sources.citation: Knobloch, Nina. 2020. A grammar sketch of Sauji: An Indo-Aryan language of Afghanistan. MA thesis, Stockholm University, Department of Linguistics. 55 pp. urn:nbn:se:su:diva-182519 (diva2:1440556). downloaded via the Internet Archive id_ capture of the DiVA open-access full text (DiVA itself could not be reached by automated download).
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request); access check: not located online or in the libraries checked
sources.note: Sec. 4.2 Phonology (pp. 12-15) covers consonants, vowels, phonotactics only. p.15 sec. 4.2.3: 'Stress and pitch accent have not been analyzed specifically in this thesis, but considering that they are phonologically relevant features in e.g. Palula (Liljegren, 2016: 72-75) and other Shina languages, they might also be of relevance for Sauji.' p.14: the -aalu ~ -aaloo past-perfective variation may correlate with stress on the preceding syllable vs. on that vowel. Sec. 5.4 p.40: 'suprasegmental phonology has not been covered in the current study'. No statement of where word stress/accent falls.

sources.citation: Strand, Richard F. Nuristân site (nuristan.info), Indo-Aryan lexicons index.
sources.note: No Sawi materials (Indo-Aryan lexicons offered: Degano Pashai, Khowar, Bhatesa, Acharetâ = Ashret Palula). Negative check.

sources.citation: Liljegren, Henrik. 2017. Profiling Indo-Aryan in the Hindukush-Karakoram: A preliminary study of micro-typological patterns. Journal of South Asian Languages and Linguistics 4(1): 107-156. doi:10.1515/jsall-2017-0004.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request); access check: open copy online (also online with a university library login)
sources.note: Sawi [sdg] is one of 31 sample languages (data: Buddruss 1967, Liljegren 2009, own data). Sec. 4.8 'Tones' pp. 122-124 reports only aggregate distributions (2-way 'Shina-type' contrast 'often described as pitch accent' is the most common type in the region); no per-language value for Sawi is printed and nothing on stress placement.

sources.citation: Liljegren, Henrik. 2009. The Dangari tongue of Choke and Machoke: Tracing the proto-language of Shina enclaves in the Hindu Kush. Acta Orientalia 70: 7-62. doi:10.5617/ao.5341 (open access).
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Sec. 6.2 'Sawi revisited' (pp. 30-32) summarizes Buddruss's (1967) Sawi phonology: consonant and vowel inventories, doubtful length contrast except a/aa, clusters; nothing on accent placement. p.34: possible connection between Palula voiced aspiration and 'low-rising pitch in Klk and Sw'. fn.25 p.28: 'the simple pitch accent system found in most other Shina varieties (including NP and SP)' (Sawi not named). Sawi items in the comparative Table 24 are written without accent marks, unlike the Palula columns. Accent placement is analysed only for Southern/Northern Palula (mora-based pitch accent)…
Nothing on stress/accent; references only Buddruss 1967, Liljegren 2009/2013, Bashir 2016a/b, Cacopardo & Cacopardo 2001, Schmidt & Kaul 2008.

sources.citation: Liljegren, Henrik et al. Hindu Kush Areal Typology (hindukush.clld.org), parameter list (274 rows incl. wordlist/kinship/numeral items and ~80 structural features).
sources.note: Sauji (fieldwork Kabul, Apr 2017) is a doculect, but the feature set contains no tone, stress or accent parameter; silent.

sources.access_detail: HathiTrust digitized, search-only (in copyright); interlibrary loan (also digitized at HathiTrust, search-only (in copyright))
sources.note: The only full primary description of Sauji with a Lautlehre (pp. 12-22); Buddruss marked pitch accent in his other Dardic/Shina work, so if any published statement on Sawi accent placement exists it is here. Neither Liljegren 2009 nor Knobloch 2020 relays one, so it must be checked directly.

sources.citation: Liljegren, Henrik. 2016. A grammar of Palula (Studies in Diversity Linguistics 8). Berlin: Language Science Press. pp. 72-75 (pitch accent).

sources.note: Open-access grammar of Sauji's closest relative; its pitch accent chapter (first/second-mora accent, lexical but morphologically conditioned shifts) is the system Knobloch says 'might also be of relevance for Sauji'; useful as the comparandum if the catalog records Sauji by proxy, but it is not a Sauji statement.
